blocks.content: Every concept covered throughout the OS course, processes, memory, files, signals, has a concrete, everyday command line counterpart on any real Linux system. This chapter is a practical field guide to the commands used constantly for inspecting, managing, and troubleshooting a running system, tying each one back to the concept it directly exposes.

None of these commands are new ideas on their own, every single one is simply a thin, practical interface onto a mechanism already covered in depth somewhere earlier in this course, ps onto the process table, chmod onto file permissions, kill onto signals, and so on.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394737-633711230.png
1. Inspecting Processes: ps and top

ps prints a one time snapshot of currently running processes, showing fields like PID, parent PID, current state, and the command that started each one, directly exposing the process table concepts from the processes and threads module. ps aux is the most common invocation, showing every process on the system regardless of which terminal, if any, started it.

top instead shows a live, continuously refreshing view of running processes, sorted by resource usage, letting an administrator watch CPU and memory consumption change in real time rather than only seeing a single static moment.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394738-315145947.png

2. File Permissions: ls, chmod, chown

ls -l lists files along with their permission bits, shown as a ten character string like rwxr-xr--, directly reflecting the permission bits stored in a file inode, tying back to the inodes chapter. The first three characters after the file type indicate the owner permissions, the next three the group permissions, and the final three everyone else.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394738-252480113.png
chmod: changing permissions numerically

chmod changes a file permission bits, and its numeric form assigns a weight to each permission, read worth 4, write worth 2, execute worth 1, summed together for each of owner, group, and other. A permission of 7 means read, write, and execute all granted, since 4 plus 2 plus 1 equals 7.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394738-407494720.png

chmod 755 script.sh
# owner: 7, read write execute
# group: 5, read and execute, no write
# other: 5, read and execute, no write

chown alice:staff report.txt
# changes the owning user to alice and the owning group to staff

blocks.content: 3. Searching: grep and find

grep and find solve two genuinely different search problems that are easy to confuse. grep searches inside the actual content of files, looking for lines that match a given text pattern, it does not care about file names at all, only what is written inside them.

find instead searches the directory tree itself, locating files by name, type, size, modification time, or other file system level attributes, it does not look inside file content at all. Reaching for the wrong one is a common early mistake, wanting to find files by name but instinctively reaching for grep, or wanting to search inside file content but reaching for find.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394738-815124866.png

grep -r "TODO" ./src          # find every line containing TODO inside ./src
find . -name "*.log"          # find every file named *.log anywhere under the current directory

blocks.content: 4. Combining Commands With Pipes

The real everyday power of these commands comes from combining them with the pipe mechanism covered in its own dedicated chapter. Piping one command output into another lets simple, single purpose tools compose into far more specific queries than any one of them could answer alone.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394739-35864317.png

ps aux | grep python      # show only processes whose command line mentions python
ls -l | grep "^d"          # show only directory entries, filtering the ls output
blocks.code:
ps aux | grep python      # show only processes whose command line mentions python
ls -l | grep "^d"          # show only directory entries, filtering the ls output

codes.bash:
ps aux | grep python      # show only processes whose command line mentions python
ls -l | grep "^d"          # show only directory entries, filtering the ls output

blocks.title: A direct application of the pipes chapter
blocks.content: Every piped command line like this is a live, everyday instance of the exact pipe mechanism explained in full, kernel buffer, one direction, blocking behavior, in the dedicated pipes chapter earlier in this module.
5. Inspecting Disk and Memory Usage

df reports free and used space per mounted file system, answering how much room is left overall on a given disk or partition. du instead reports how much space a specific file or directory is actually using, answering a much more targeted question about one particular piece of the file system.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394739-603110345.png

free reports current memory usage system wide, how much RAM is in use, how much is free, and how much swap space, tying directly back to the swapping chapter, is currently in use, a quick way to spot memory pressure or active thrashing symptoms from the thrashing chapter.

6. Sending Signals: kill

kill sends a signal to a process by PID, directly exercising the signals chapter mechanism from the command line. Called with no flags, it sends SIGTERM, a polite request the target process can catch and handle before exiting cleanly. Called with -9, it sends SIGKILL, forcing immediate termination that cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored under any circumstances.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409394739-234760008.png
7. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Reaching for grep to search for files by name, or find to search inside file content, when each tool solves a genuinely different one of those two problems.","Reaching straight for kill -9 out of habit, when a plain kill sending SIGTERM first gives the target process a real chance to clean up, exactly the distinction covered in the signals chapter.","Confusing df, which reports space at the file system level, with du, which reports space used by a specific file or directory, they answer genuinely different questions."]
items: Reaching for grep to search for files by name, or find to search inside file content, when each tool solves a genuinely different one of those two problems.
Reaching straight for kill -9 out of habit, when a plain kill sending SIGTERM first gives the target process a real chance to clean up, exactly the distinction covered in the signals chapter.
Confusing df, which reports space at the file system level, with du, which reports space used by a specific file or directory, they answer genuinely different questions.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain what a handful of these commands actually do at the OS level, not just what flags to pass, being able to say ps reads the kernel process table and chmod modifies bits stored directly in a file inode shows real understanding, not memorized syntax.

Every command in this chapter is a thin, practical window onto a mechanism already explained in depth earlier in this course. The final chapters in this module bring everything together with a consolidated set of the most frequently asked OS interview questions and a compact cheat sheet.
